title: Where you hold it
hook: stress often lands in the jaw, shoulders or belly

segments.voice: Yesterday, kayagatasati, feet to head, noticing without fixing. Your line was here I am. What did you find on the way up? Day one hundred thirty-three.

Try this, right now, without changing anything first. Where are your shoulders? Are they sitting low and easy, or have they crept up toward your ears? And your teeth: touching, or pressed together? And your belly: soft, or pulled in like you're bracing for a hit? Often at least one of them turns out to be on duty, holding something, for no reason anyone could name. That's what yesterday's scan was quietly turning up. Today we get specific. Today's practice is where you hold it.
screen: `SHOULDERS BY YOUR EARS?` → `TEETH PRESSED TOGETHER?` → `WHERE YOU HOLD IT.`

segments.voice: Here's what's going on. When the body senses a threat, it gets ready. In a 1915 book, the American physiologist Walter Cannon described that readiness for fighting or for flight, and fight or flight is the name that stuck. The heart speeds up, breathing quickens, and muscles tighten, ready to strike or run. That's useful if there's a bear. The trouble is that a hard email, a traffic jam or a tense dinner can set off a smaller version of the same thing, and there's nothing to strike and nowhere to run. So the tension just stays. And it tends to settle in the same few places. The jaw: some people clench their teeth when stressed, often without knowing, some even in their sleep. The shoulders: they rise and round forward, a little like a turtle pulling in. And the belly: the muscles brace, and breathing moves up into the chest. In 1929, a Chicago doctor named Edmund Jacobson published a book called Progressive Relaxation. His discovery was simple: people often can't feel how tense a muscle is until they first tighten it on purpose, and then let go. The contrast teaches the body what soft feels like. None of this needs a teacher or a mat. It needs a habit of checking. These three places are where a hard day tends to show. You can check them, and you can let them go, one muscle at a time.
screen: `FIGHT OR FLIGHT, 1915.` · `THE BEAR THAT ISN'T THERE.` · `JAW, SHOULDERS, BELLY.` · `TIGHTEN, THEN LET GO.` · then, large: `LET THE SHOULDERS DOWN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: soften the jaw, drop the shoulders. First the jaw. Let your teeth part a little, lips closed, tongue resting. Now the shoulders: lift them toward your ears on purpose, hold for a breath, and let them fall. Feel the difference. Do it once more. Then the belly: let it go soft, and let the breath drop down into it. Stay there, loose, and each time something tightens, notice, and let it down again. The bell holds the time.
Jacobson. The doctor who found that tensing a muscle on purpose, then letting go, teaches the body what soft feels like. Today's word.
Your line: let the shoulders down. Today, every time you open a message, check your shoulders and your jaw, and let them go. Day one hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: Some people use progressive muscle relaxation, tensing and then releasing each muscle group in turn, and relaxation courses often teach a quick check of the jaw, shoulders and belly during the day.

fork.setup: you can't tell if your shoulders are tense. what does Jacobson's method say to do?
options: ignore it; if you can't feel it, it's fine.
tighten them on purpose, then let go.
stretch as hard as you can.
fork.reveal: tighten on purpose, hold, and let go. the contrast teaches the body what soft feels like.

trapdoor: what you thought: tense shoulders just mean a bad chair.
what it means: stress readies the body, and the tension settles in the jaw, shoulders and belly.
what a scholar hears: Cannon's fight-or-flight (1915) and Jacobson's Progressive Relaxation (1929), which taught release by first tightening on purpose.

sources.ref: Bodily Changes in Pain, Hunger, Fear and Rage (1915)

notes: Cannon is widely credited with 'fight or flight' in the 1915 book; confirm the phrase appears there.
Jacobson's Progressive Relaxation, 1929, University of Chicago Press: confirm date and his Chicago base.
Stress-related jaw clenching (awake and sleep bruxism) is stated generally; a health reviewer may want to check wording.
No original-language word: original is null.

Editor review 2026-10-01: Cannon now 'described' the fight-or-flight readiness in 1915 rather than being credited with the exact phrase; 'most people who check' and 'many people clench' softened; replaced 'your body is keeping score' (echoes a modern book title; stock phrase) with a concrete line.
